y-m-68-01.title: When n is very large, can we say √(n²+4n) equals n?
y-m-68-01.topic: Limit of a sequence: guessing and checking a sequence with a square root
y-m-68-01.goal: When guessing the limit of a sequence with a square root, tell apart whether "almost equal" is true as a ratio (relative size) or as a difference (absolute gap), and revise your guess and your degree of confidence each time new numerical data comes out.
y-m-68-01.material: You want to find out the limit of the sequence a_n = √(n² + 4n) − n (n = 1, 2, 3, …). (Read as: square root of n squared plus 4n, minus n.) One student guessed this: "When n is very large, 4n is almost nothing compared with n². Then √(n²+4n) is almost the same as √(n²) = n, so if you subtract n it will get close to 0." Let's think about what happens to this guess while looking at the data one piece at a time. The values from the calculator are written to four decimal places.
y-m-68-01.thinking.0: Treat the first guess as a hypothesis to test rather than settling it
y-m-68-01.thinking.1: Revise your judgment and degree of confidence with new data
y-m-68-01.thinking.2: Tell apart the ratio (relative size) from the difference (absolute gap)
y-m-68-01.prereq.0: The meaning of the limit of a sequence: as n grows without bound, the terms get closer and closer to one value
y-m-68-01.prereq.1: The experience of estimating the value of an expression with a square root using a calculator
y-m-68-01.prereq.2: Assumption: after learning the sequence limit unit of high school Calculus II (H3 is a difficulty classification of this set of tasks and does not mean assignment to a specific grade)
y-m-68-01.s.s1.prompt: The data is revealed one step at a time. At each step, choose what you think now. You do not have to keep what you chose in an earlier step.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.hint.0: First look at how the numbers in the table move as n changes (do they grow, shrink, or stop?).
y-m-68-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the student's guess (the limit is 0) and the values in the table agree with each other.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.info: There are no calculated values yet. There is only the student's guess (the limit is 0).
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.ask: How will you treat this guess right now?
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.after: Right now it is fitting to treat the guess as a "hypothesis to test" or to hold back judgment. It is too early to settle on 0 (a) when there is no evidence.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 0 is right. 4n is small compared with n², so there is no need to check the values separately.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Saying it is small compared with n² is a statement about a ratio. What is left after subtracting is a difference, so it is too early to settle without checking.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It might be 0, but I will calculate the value at a few n and check.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You did not settle the guess and treated it as a hypothesis to test.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I think a sequence with a square root has no limit.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.r.c: There are many sequences with square roots that do have a limit. You cannot generalize that there is no limit because of a square root.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.o.d: I have no grounds to guess yet, so I will first calculate values and then think.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is the choice to hold back judgment and gather data first when there are no grounds.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.ask: Looking at these values, what do you think about the limit now?
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.after: At n = 10 it is already 1.83, so the guess "it gets close to 0" does not fit the data. Still, from the values up to 10 alone, you cannot decide what value it approaches or whether it grows without bound. It is fitting to revise the guess, keep your confidence low, and look at larger n.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is still 0. n is still small, and when it gets larger it will come down to 0.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It is not completely impossible, but the values are moving farther and farther from 0. The data gives no grounds for saying it will come down.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The values keep growing, so I think it is a sequence that grows without bound.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The observation that the values are growing is right. But whether the growth slows down must be seen at larger n. It is too early to decide now that it grows without bound.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It doesn't seem to be 0. To know what value it approaches, I need values at larger n.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You admitted that the first guess does not fit the data and left what you do not know yet open.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It seems to approach somewhere near 2, but I'm not sure, so I will check at larger n.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You made a new guess from the data and also kept your degree of confidence low.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.ask: What will you say about the limit now?
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.after: The values in the table approach 2. The first guess (0) does not fit the data and has to be revised. However, the table has rounded values, so it is not a proof. It becomes more certain if you go on to check by transforming the expression. (For example, writing a_n = 4n / (√(n²+4n) + n) lets you work out the limit.)
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The limit is 0. As I first thought, this is because 4n is small compared with n².
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.r.a: "Small compared with n²" means the ratio of √(n²+4n) to n is close to 1. When you subtract, what is left is a difference, not a ratio, and the values in the table show that the difference is near 2.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The limit is probably a value close to 2. The values approach 2, so I will check with an expression too.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You formed a new conclusion from the values in the table and also took care that a table is not a proof.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The limit does not exist. This is because the values keep changing and do not stop at one value.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.r.c: A limit does not mean the value stops; it means it gets closer and closer. Even if it keeps changing, if it approaches 2 there is a limit.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The limit is 2. The table shows 2.0000, so there is no need to check separately, and it is settled.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The conclusion of 2 is a strong clue. But a rounded table is not a proof, so the table alone cannot rule out the possibility of another value very close to 2.
y-m-68-01.s.s1.reflect: When did the first guess (0) get revised, once what data came out? Why was it important that you did not settle on 0 before that? How was your degree of confidence different when the data went only up to n=10 and when it went up to n=100000?
y-m-68-01.s.s2.prompt: The guess that did not fit the data, "√(n²+4n) is almost the same as n," is right in one sense and wrong in another. Choose the most fitting explanation.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.hint.0: Estimate √(n²+4n) and n at n = 100 and write both the value you get by dividing the two numbers and the value you get by subtracting.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.hint.1: For the same two numbers, compare where the "divided value" and the "subtracted value" each go as n grows.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.o.a: Even as n grows, 4n does not get smaller, so the idea of ignoring 4n is itself wrong.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.r.a: 4n grows, but the ratio 4/n compared with n² gets close to 0. The statement "it is small by comparison" is right. The problem is that it was used for a difference.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.o.b: n²+4n is not a perfect square, so the root cannot be simplified, and no size comparison can be made.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.r.b: Even if it is not a perfect square, a size comparison can be made. For example, n² < n²+4n < (n+2)², so you can trap the value.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.o.c: The ratio of the two numbers gets close to 1, but the difference of the two numbers gets close to a value that is not 0. A statement that is right for the ratio was used for the difference.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.r.c: You told apart ratio and difference and sorted out in which sense the guess is right and in which it is wrong.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.o.d: √(n²+4n) is exactly equal to n+2, so the subtracted value is always 2 and does not depend on n.
y-m-68-01.s.s2.r.d: (n+2)² = n²+4n+4, so √(n²+4n) is a little smaller than n+2. The subtracted value is not always 2; it only gets close to 2 (the values in the table are also less than 2).
y-m-68-01.s.s2.explain: The ratio √(n²+4n)/n = √(1+4/n) gets close to 1, but the difference gets close to 2. n²+4n is 4 less than (n+2)², so √(n²+4n) is a little smaller than n+2, and so it is bigger than n by about 2.
y-m-68-01.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to send to the student who made the first guess. Say what the limit gets close to (not 0), and explain in what sense "almost the same" is right and in what sense it is wrong. (2 to 4 sentences)
y-m-68-01.s.s3.hint.0: Imagine underlining the parts of the student's words that are right, and look at whether each part is about the "divided value" or the "subtracted value."
y-m-68-01.s.s3.hint.1: Say, using the values in the table, how much bigger √(n²+4n) is than n when n is 10000.
y-m-68-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say both the sense in which "almost the same" is right (the ratio) and the sense in which it is wrong (the difference)?
y-m-68-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: As grounds that the limit is near 2, not 0, did you cite the values in the table or an expression like n+2?
y-m-68-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Without ignoring the student's idea, did you acknowledge how far it is right?
y-m-68-01.s.s3.model.0: 4n is small compared with n, so the ratio of √(n²+4n) to n gets close to 1. So "almost the same" is right as a ratio. But when you subtract n, what is left is a difference, not a ratio. When n=10000, √(n²+4n) is bigger than n by about 2, so the limit is 2, not 0.
y-m-68-01.s.s3.model.1: √(n²+4n) is a number just a little smaller than n+2, so it is bigger than n by about 2. If you look at the divided value they look almost the same, but the subtracted difference gets close to 2, so a_n gets close to 2.
y-m-68-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: This told them apart as "divided value" without using the word "ratio."

y-m-68-02.title: Where is the r that makes the limit 5?
y-m-68-02.topic: Limit of a sequence: a limit that depends on the size of the common ratio r (splitting into cases)
y-m-68-02.goal: Split into cases using the fact that the behavior of r^n depends on the size of r, make several different r for which the limit is 5, and do not miss the surprising case (when r is greater than 1).
y-m-68-02.material: For a positive number r, consider the sequence a_n = (r^(n+1) + 5) / (r^n + 1) (n = 1, 2, 3, …). (Read as: the numerator is "r to the power n+1, plus 5," and the denominator is "r to the power n, plus 1.") When the value of r changes, the limit of this sequence can change too. This time you will try to make an r for which the limit is 5. r is a real number greater than 0.
y-m-68-02.thinking.1: Make and check several examples that meet the condition
y-m-68-02.thinking.2: Find an unexpected solution and confirm it with a reason
y-m-68-02.prereq.0: The behavior of the sequence r^n for positive r: if 0<r<1 it gets close to 0, if r=1 it is 1, and if r>1 it grows without bound
y-m-68-02.prereq.1: The experience of finding the limit of a sequence in fraction form
y-m-68-02.prereq.2: Assumption: right after the sequence limit unit of high school Calculus II (H3 is a difficulty classification of this set of tasks and does not mean assignment to a specific grade)
y-m-68-02.s.s1.prompt: First check how r^n behaves. Choose all the r for which r^n gets closer and closer to 0 as n grows without bound.
y-m-68-02.s.s1.hint.0: For r = 0.5, calculate the values of r, r², r³ in order.
y-m-68-02.s.s1.hint.1: Split into the case where r is less than 1 and the case where it is greater, write only a few terms of each in a table, and compare.
y-m-68-02.s.s1.r.a: It keeps halving, like 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, …, and gets close to 0.
y-m-68-02.s.s1.r.b: 1 stays 1 no matter how many times you raise it to a power, so it does not get close to 0.
y-m-68-02.s.s1.r.c: Even if it is very close to 1, like 1.01, if it is greater than 1 the powers grow without bound, even if very slowly.
y-m-68-02.s.s1.r.d: Even if it is close to 1, like 0.99, if it is less than 1 the powers get close to 0 (very slowly).
y-m-68-02.s.s1.explain: r^n gets close to 0 if 0<r<1, stays at 1 if r=1, and grows without bound if r>1. Thinking in these three cases is the starting point of this task.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different values of r for which the limit is 5.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a few r and calculate the terms at large n yourself. At which r is it near 5?
y-m-68-02.s.s2.hint.1: When r is greater than 1, compare which term in the numerator and the denominator grows fastest.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.ok.c2: With this r, the limit of the sequence is 5.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.fail.c2: With this r, the limit does not become 5. Split into when r is less than 1, when it is 1, and when it is greater than 1, and work out what the limit is in each.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.explain: If 0<r<1, r^n gets close to 0, so the limit is 5/1 = 5. So every positive number less than 1, like 0.5, 0.1, 0.99, works. If r = 1 the limit is (1+5)/(1+1) = 3, and if r>1 the limit is r, so it is 5 only when r = 5. In fact, if r = 5, a_n = 5 for every n.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Is there a case where the limit is 5 even though r is greater than 1? If there is, write which r it is; if not, write why not, with the reason.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Calculate a few terms with values like r = 2, r = 3, r = 10 and compare in a table where the limit goes.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Say what relationship between the limit and r you can see in that table.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: if r is greater than 1, ...
y-m-68-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the reason the limit becomes r when r is greater than 1 (comparing the largest terms of the numerator and denominator)?
y-m-68-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you check that if r = 5 the sequence is actually constant at 5?
y-m-68-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you write the case r<1 and the case r>1 separately?
y-m-68-02.s.s2.because.model.0: Yes, there is. If r is greater than 1, dividing the numerator and denominator by r^n shows the limit is r, so when r = 5 the limit is 5. In fact, if r = 5, (5^(n+1)+5)/(5^n+1) is constant at 5 for every n.
y-m-68-02.s.s2.because.model.1: There is: r = 5. If r is greater than 1, the limit goes toward r, so for the limit to be 5, r must be 5. A number greater than 1 other than 5, for example 2, has limit 2, so it does not work.

y-m-68-03.title: What value do you need to know the slope of an inverse function?
y-m-68-03.topic: Various differentiation methods: the information needed to fix the derivative value of an inverse function
y-m-68-03.goal: Sort out the necessary and unnecessary information for finding the inverse function's derivative value g'(3), and tell apart which "value at which point" the same information can fix.
y-m-68-03.material:
The function f is differentiable on all real numbers, and f'(x) > 0 for every x. So f has an inverse function g, and g is also differentiable. That is, g(f(x)) = x for every x. A student wrote down known values of f on cards in order to find the value of g'(3). All the cards are facts.
Card ① f(1) = 3
Card ② f'(1) = 5
Card ③ f'(3) = 29
Card ④ f(3) = 33
The formula is not known, and only these four pieces of information are available. (Read as: f prime of 1, g prime of 3.)
y-m-68-03.thinking.0: Judge whether information is necessary and sufficient
y-m-68-03.thinking.1: Find the wrong line in a solution
y-m-68-03.thinking.2: Tell apart values that can and cannot be fixed with the given information (tell inputs and outputs apart)
y-m-68-03.prereq.0: The meaning that the derivative is the instantaneous rate of change at one point (the slope of the tangent line)
y-m-68-03.prereq.1: The meaning that the inverse function g satisfies g(f(x)) = x
y-m-68-03.prereq.2: Assumption: after learning the differentiation unit of high school Calculus II (H3 is a difficulty classification of this set of tasks and does not mean assignment to a specific grade)
y-m-68-03.s.s1.prompt: To fix the value of g'(3), which of the cards are absolutely needed? Choose all the cards that are needed.
y-m-68-03.s.s1.hint.0: In g'(3), the 3 is an input of g. Find on the cards what g gives back (an input of f) when the input of g is 3.
y-m-68-03.s.s1.hint.1: Look for a card that tells you the slope at that input of f.
y-m-68-03.s.s1.r.a: f'(3) is the slope when the input of f is 3. In g'(3), the 3 is an input of g and an output of f. You are reading input and output the wrong way round.
y-m-68-03.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out that if there is an input of f that corresponds to the input 3 of g, you need information about the slope of f at that point.
y-m-68-03.s.s1.r.c: f(3) = 33 is information about the point where the input of g is 33 (g(33) = 3). It is different from the point where the input of g is 3.
y-m-68-03.s.s1.r.d: f(1) = 3 means g(3) = 1. It tells you where the input of f is that corresponds to the input 3 of g.
y-m-68-03.s.s1.explain: g'(3) is the slope when the input of g is 3. Since f(1) = 3, the input of f that corresponds to that point is 1, and there you need the slope of f, f'(1) = 5. Then g'(3) = 1/f'(1) = 1/5. Cards ③ and ④ are information when the input of f is 3, so they speak about a different point from g'(3).
y-m-68-03.s.s2.prompt: Another student says they found g'(3) using only card ③. Choose the line in the solution where the problem first occurs.
y-m-68-03.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether the number inside g'( ) in line 4 is really 3, by putting 3 for x in the form g'(f(x)) in line 3.
y-m-68-03.s.s2.hint.1: Find the value of f(3) on the cards and compare it with the number inside g'( ).
y-m-68-03.s.s2.line.0: g is the inverse function of f, so g(f(x)) = x for every x.
y-m-68-03.s.s2.line.1: Differentiating both sides with respect to x gives g'(f(x)) · f'(x) = 1.
y-m-68-03.s.s2.line.3: We need g'(3), so putting in x = 3 gives g'(3) = 1 / f'(3).
y-m-68-03.s.s2.line.4: From card ③, f'(3) = 29, so g'(3) = 1/29.
y-m-68-03.s.s2.explain: It is line 4. Putting in x = 3 gives g'(f(3)) = 1/f'(3), but f(3) = 33, so this is the value of g'(33). To get g'(3), you must put in the x with f(x) = 3 (= 1). Lines 1 to 3 are right.
y-m-68-03.s.s3.prompt: Suppose you know only card ③ f'(3) = 29 and card ④ f(3) = 33. Which value can be fixed with these two pieces of information?
y-m-68-03.s.s3.hint.0: Rewrite f(3) = 33 as a statement about g.
y-m-68-03.s.s3.hint.1: When the slope of f is large, think about what the slope becomes when you look at the same point on the graph of g, by picturing the graph flipped over the line y = x, and compare.
y-m-68-03.s.s3.r.a: g'(3) is the slope at the point where the input of g is 3, but these two cards are information about the point where the input of f is 3 (the output is 33).
y-m-68-03.s.s3.r.b: The slope of an inverse function is the reciprocal of the original slope. It becomes one twenty-ninth, not 29.
y-m-68-03.s.s3.r.c: 29 is a slope and 33 is a function value, and their roles got mixed up. A slope cannot go in the place of an input of g.
y-m-68-03.s.s3.r.d: From f(3) = 33 you read the input 33 of g, and you changed the slope to its reciprocal, linking the two cards appropriately.
y-m-68-03.s.s3.explain: If f(3) = 33 then g(33) = 3, and the slope at that point is the reciprocal of f'(3). So g'(33) = 1/29. What these two cards tell you is the slope when the input of g is 33, and to say anything about g'(3) you need cards ① and ②.

y-m-68-04.title: A curve that passes through the origin twice: is the tangent line just one?
y-m-68-04.topic: Various differentiation methods: tangent lines to a curve given by a parameter (same point, different tangent lines)
y-m-68-04.goal: Learn that the coordinates of a point alone may not fix a single tangent line of a curve given by a parameter, make several parameter values that meet a condition yourself, and say what more you need to know.
y-m-68-04.material: A curve C is given for a real number t by x = t² − 9, y = (t³ − 9t)/3. As t changes, the point (x, y) moves along the curve. For example, if t = 0, the point is (−9, 0). t = 3 and t = −3 both pass through the origin (0, 0). While t moves from −3 to 3, the point leaves the origin, goes around a loop once on the left side where x ≤ 0, and returns to the origin. So the curve meets itself at the origin. The slope of the tangent line is fixed by the direction the point is moving at t (but you can speak of a slope only at points where x changes along with t).
y-m-68-04.thinking.0: Judge whether information is sufficient (is it the coordinates of a point or a parameter value?)
y-m-68-04.thinking.1: Make several parameter values that meet a condition
y-m-68-04.thinking.2: Test a generalization with a counterexample (same point, different tangent lines)
y-m-68-04.prereq.0: That each parameter t corresponds to one point on the curve
y-m-68-04.prereq.1: How to solve a quadratic equation
y-m-68-04.prereq.2: Assumption: after learning the differentiation unit of high school Calculus II (curves given by a parameter) (H3 is a difficulty classification of this set of tasks and does not mean assignment to a specific grade)
y-m-68-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the fitting statement about the slope of the tangent line of the curve C at the origin.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.hint.0: Find all the t for which x = 0.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.hint.1: At each t you found, separately write the direction the point is moving (whether x and y are increasing or decreasing) and compare.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.o.a: The origin is the point where x = 0, so t = 0, and then the rate at which x changes is 0, so the slope of the tangent line cannot be determined.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.r.a: The t for which x = 0 come from t² = 9, so t = 3 or t = −3. t = 0 is the point (−9, 0), not the origin.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.o.b: The origin is passed twice, at t = 3 and at t = −3, and the slope differs each time, so the coordinates of the point alone cannot give a single slope.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.r.b: You told apart at which t the curve passes through even the same point, and looked separately at the tangent lines at the point passed twice.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.o.c: The origin is passed at t = 3, so the slope is fixed as one value. t = −3 just counts the same point once more.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.r.c: The direction in which the curve passes through the origin at t = −3 is different from that at t = 3. Even at the same point, if the direction of passing is different, the tangent line can be different.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.o.d: The origin is a point where y = 0 and the curve crosses the x-axis, so the slope of the tangent line is 0.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.r.d: The curve meeting the x-axis does not mean the tangent line is parallel to the x-axis. You have to look separately at the direction of motion at that point.
y-m-68-04.s.s1.explain: At t = 3, the rate of change of x is 6 and the rate of change of y is 6, so the slope is 1, and at t = −3 the rate of change of x is −6 and the rate of change of y is 6, so the slope is −1. At the same point (0, 0) there are two tangent lines (y = x, y = −x). So "the slope at the origin" is fixed only when the parameter value (at which time it passes) is stated too.
y-m-68-04.s.s2.prompt: Make a point that has a tangent line with slope 1, using 2 different values of t.
y-m-68-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write the rate at which y changes and the rate at which x changes as expressions in t, and rewrite "the slope is 1" as a relationship between the two expressions.
y-m-68-04.s.s2.hint.1: Check what kind of equation in t the expression you got is, and guess how many solutions it will have.
y-m-68-04.s.s2.ok.c1: At this t, x changes along with t, so you can speak of a slope.
y-m-68-04.s.s2.fail.c1: At t = 0, the rate at which x changes is 0, so the slope is not determined (a vertical tangent line).
y-m-68-04.s.s2.ok.c2: At this t, the slope of the tangent line is 1.
y-m-68-04.s.s2.fail.c2: At this t, the slope of the tangent line is not 1. Write the rate at which y changes and the rate at which x changes at this t, and check whether their ratio is 1.
y-m-68-04.s.s2.explain: They are t = 3 and t = −1. t = 3 is the origin, and t = −1 is the point (−8, 8/3). Tangent lines with slope 1 occur at two different points. They are the two roots of t² − 2t − 3 = 0.
y-m-68-04.s.s3.prompt: A friend said, "There is only one place on the curve where the tangent line has slope 1." Answer your friend using the two values you made above, and also write what more you would have to be told to speak of the tangent line at the origin as a single line.
y-m-68-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write the coordinates of the points that correspond to the two t values you made above.
y-m-68-04.s.s3.hint.1: For the origin, compare how many t correspond to it and whether the slopes at each are the same.
y-m-68-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: the places where the slope is 1 are ...
y-m-68-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say that there are two places with slope 1 (t = 3 and t = −1)?
y-m-68-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why the tangent line at the origin is not fixed to one (the slopes are 1 and −1 at t = 3 and t = −3)?
y-m-68-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say what more you need to know not as a "point" but as a "parameter value or the direction of passing"?
y-m-68-04.s.s3.model.0: It is not just one place. t = 3 is the origin and t = −1 is the point (−8, 8/3). Both have slope 1, so there are two places. And to speak of the tangent line at the origin as a single line, you would have to be told more, namely whether it passes with t = 3 or with t = −3, that is, the direction of passing.
y-m-68-04.s.s3.model.1: The same slope can come from two different points on the curve. Besides, the origin is passed twice, at t = 3 and t = −3, so the slopes differ, 1 and −1. So the coordinates of the point alone are not enough, and you need the parameter value.

y-m-68-05.title: Solving the definite integral of x·e^(x²): where did it go off?
y-m-68-05.topic: Integration methods: checking the interval of integration after changing to a new letter in a definite integral
y-m-68-05.goal: Find the line where the interval went wrong in a finished solution, judge that both splitting the interval and calculating in one go are valid, and sift out a wrong value by estimation without calculating.
y-m-68-05.material: A student solved the definite integral ∫ x·e^(x²) dx (from x = −1 to 2) in the 4 lines below. (Read as: x times e to the power of x squared, dx.) For reference, e ≈ 2.718.
y-m-68-05.thinking.0: Find where the error is in a solution
y-m-68-05.thinking.1: Compare the validity of two different solutions
y-m-68-05.thinking.2: Check the validity of an answer by estimation
y-m-68-05.prereq.0: That the indefinite integral of e^x is e^x
y-m-68-05.prereq.1: The form of calculating a definite integral as F(b) − F(a) using an indefinite integral F
y-m-68-05.prereq.2: That e^(x²) is a function that has x² as its exponent (calculating function values)
y-m-68-05.prereq.3: Assumption: during the integration methods unit of high school Calculus II (H3 is a difficulty classification of this set of tasks and does not mean assignment to a specific grade)
y-m-68-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in the student's solution where it first goes wrong. (Some lines have correct calculations.)
y-m-68-05.s.s1.hint.0: Put x = −1 and x = 2 into u = x² and find the values of u.
y-m-68-05.s.s1.hint.1: In line 2, work out from the range of values x² can take whether there can be a moment when u is −1.
y-m-68-05.s.s1.line.0: Letting u = x², we get du = 2x dx, so x dx = (1/2) du.
y-m-68-05.s.s1.line.1: x changes from −1 to 2, so u also changes from −1 to 2.
y-m-68-05.s.s1.line.2: Therefore the given definite integral is the definite integral of (1/2)·e^u du from u = −1 to 2.
y-m-68-05.s.s1.explain: It is line 2. Since u = x², when x = −1, u = 1, and when x = 2, u = 4. Besides, x² is at least 0, so u cannot be −1. If you change the interval to values of u, you get (1/2)[e^u] (from u = 1 to 4) = (e⁴ − e)/2. Line 1 is right, and lines 3 and 4 are results that follow the interval in line 2.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.prompt: Another student said this: "x² decreases from x = −1 to 0 and increases from 0 to 2, so it does not move in only one direction. So you can't change to u = 1 to 4 in one go, and you must split the interval at x = 0." Calculating by splitting gives (1 − e)/2 + (e⁴ − 1)/2, and changing in one go gives (e⁴ − e)/2, and the two values are equal. Choose the fitting judgment about this situation.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.hint.0: Compare where the value of u at x = 0 (which is 0) is used in each of the two methods.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.hint.1: Write out for yourself what happens to the e^0 terms when you split and add.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.o.a: The one-go value coming out the same is a coincidence, so the method that does not split the interval is a wrong method.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.r.a: The same value is not a coincidence. The expression has the form e^u multiplied by the rate of change of u (2x), so the two methods are built to give the same value.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.o.b: If u does not move in only one direction, this definite integral cannot be solved by changing to u.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.r.b: The solution calculated by splitting also used the same u. If it could not be used, the split solution would have to be wrong too.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.o.c: The values of the two methods are equal, so it does not matter if the rule of changing the interval to values of u is wrong.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.r.c: The rule is not right because the values are equal; it is right because there is a reason to change to the values u takes at the ends of the interval. The error in step 1 was an error that made the value different.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.o.d: Changing in one go is fine and calculating by splitting is not wrong either. What matters is using the values u takes at the ends of the interval.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.r.d: You explained why both splitting the interval and doing it in one go are fine by the values of u at the ends of the interval.
y-m-68-05.s.s2.explain: x e^(x²) has the form e^u multiplied by (1/2)·(the rate of change of u), so even if u goes up and down, you can change to the values of u at the ends of the interval (1 and 4) and calculate in one go. The part where u goes down to 0 and comes back up connects up in the split calculation and gives the same value. Calculating by splitting is not necessary, but it is not wrong either.
y-m-68-05.s.s3.prompt: Show, by estimating without calculating the definite integral, that the value of the wrong solution, (e² − e^(−1))/2 ≈ 3.5, cannot be the right value. Write it with a specific range of x and specific numbers. (Reference: e^2.25 ≈ 9.5, e^3.24 ≈ 25.5. Also take care that the part where x is from −1 to 0 has negative values.)
y-m-68-05.s.s3.hint.0: Find the values at x = 1, 1.5, 2 and compare how the value of x·e^(x²) changes as x gets larger.
y-m-68-05.s.s3.hint.1: Make one rectangle using the smaller value, such as the value at the left end of the interval, and estimate the area.
y-m-68-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: when x is from ... to ..., x·e^(x²) is ...
y-m-68-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you take a lower bound of the function value on part of the interval and build a lower bound for the integral?
y-m-68-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you also work out how large the effect of the interval where the value is negative (from −1 to 0) could be?
y-m-68-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you compare the estimated value directly with 3.5?
y-m-68-05.s.s3.model.0: When x is between 1.5 and 2, x·e^(x²) is at least 1.5·e^2.25 ≈ 14, so multiplying by the interval length 0.5, the integral is at least 7. The negative part from −1 to 0 has size at most e, so it lowers it by at most about 2.7, and it is still over 4. It is larger than 3.5, so it is a wrong value.
y-m-68-05.s.s3.model.1: When x is between 1.8 and 2, the function value is at least 1.8·e^3.24 ≈ 46, so even multiplied by the interval length 0.2 it is at least 9. However large the negative part is, it is about 2.7, so the total is larger than 6. 3.5 is too small.

y-m-68-06.title: The derivative of x^x: whose words are right, of the two students?
y-m-68-06.topic: Various differentiation methods: judging two formulas for the derivative of x^x using evidence
y-m-68-06.goal: Learn the case where numerical data at one point cannot separate two derivative formulas, make a counterexample that sifts out the wrong formula using function values alone, and explain why the wrong formula looks right by coincidence at one point.
y-m-68-06.material:
Two students found the derivative of f(x) = x^x (x > 0). (Read as: x to the power of x.)
Student A: "The exponent is x, so in (x^n)′ = n·x^(n−1), put x in the place of n, and f′(x) = x·x^(x−1) = x^x."
Student B: "Taking the natural logarithm of both sides, ln f = x·ln x, and differentiating gives f′/f = ln x + 1, so f′(x) = x^x·(ln x + 1)."
To check which is right, the average rate of change at x = 1, (f(1.001) − f(1)) / 0.001, was found with a calculator and came to about 1.0010.
y-m-68-06.thinking.0: Tell apart what evidence can and cannot decide
y-m-68-06.thinking.1: Make a counterexample to a derivative formula using function values alone
y-m-68-06.thinking.2: Explain the conditions for applying a rule and a coincidental agreement
y-m-68-06.prereq.0: The meaning that the derivative is the instantaneous rate of change at one point (the slope of the tangent line)
y-m-68-06.prereq.1: How to find the value of x^x for x > 0 with a calculator
y-m-68-06.prereq.2: Assumption: after learning the differentiation unit of high school Calculus II (H3 is a difficulty classification of this set of tasks and does not mean assignment to a specific grade)
y-m-68-06.s.s1.prompt: Which of A and B does the data that the average rate of change at x = 1 is about 1.0010 support?
y-m-68-06.s.s1.hint.0: Put x = 1 into each student's formula and compare the values.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.hint.1: Say what the two formulas would have to be like at that point for the data to separate them.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.o.a: It supports only A. A's formula is 1 at x = 1 and the data is also close to 1.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.r.a: That is true, but B's formula is also 1·(ln 1 + 1) = 1 at x = 1. To say it supports only one formula, the other formula would have to not match this data.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.o.b: It supports only B. B went as far as using logarithms and is the more careful method, so it matches the data.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.r.b: A method being complicated does not make the result right. You have to compare the data with the value of each formula directly.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.o.c: It matches both. The two formulas give the same value at x = 1, so this data cannot separate them.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.r.c: You put x = 1 into each formula, compared the values, and worked out whether the data separates the two formulas.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.o.d: Both are wrong. An interval of 0.001 is an approximation, so it does not match any formula.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.r.d: The average rate of change over an interval of 0.001 is an approximation that comes out very close to the slope of the tangent line. 1.0010 and 1 are almost the same.
y-m-68-06.s.s1.explain: A's formula x^x and B's formula x^x(ln x + 1) are both 1 at x = 1 because ln 1 = 0. If data at one point matches both formulas, that data cannot separate the two formulas. To separate them, you need data at a point where the values of the two formulas are different from each other.
y-m-68-06.s.s2.prompt: If A's formula f′(x) = x^x were really right, there is something that must happen for f. Make 2 different pairs of numbers 0 < p < q for which that does not happen. (Use only the values f(p) = p^p and f(q) = q^q.)
y-m-68-06.s.s2.hint.0: Make a table of the values of x^x at x equal to 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1 and see how it moves.
y-m-68-06.s.s2.hint.1: Since A's formula is always positive, think about what must follow about whether the function grows or shrinks as you go to the right.
y-m-68-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make it so that 0 < p < q.
y-m-68-06.s.s2.ok.c2: p^p is larger than q^q, so the value of f decreases going from p to q.
y-m-68-06.s.s2.fail.c2: For these two numbers p^p ≤ q^q, so you cannot see f decreasing. Compare the values of x^x at several x with a calculator.
y-m-68-06.s.s2.explain: For example, f(0.1) ≈ 0.794 and f(0.5) ≈ 0.707, so f decreases while going from 0.1 to 0.5. But A's formula x^x is positive for every x > 0, so f should only increase, which is a contradiction. So A's formula is wrong. (The place where f decreases is the side where 0 < x < 1/e.)
y-m-68-06.s.s3.prompt: Explain why A's formula happened to look right at x = 1, and what rule A used in a place where it does not fit. (2 to 3 sentences)
y-m-68-06.s.s3.hint.0: Recall what kind of number n was when you first learned (x^n)′ = n·x^(n−1).
y-m-68-06.s.s3.hint.1: Find the x where A's formula x^x and B's formula x^x(ln x + 1) become equal.
y-m-68-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you point out that (x^n)′ = n·x^(n−1) is a rule used when the exponent n is a constant?
y-m-68-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say why the two formulas have the same value at x = 1 (ln 1 = 0)?
y-m-68-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you give a reason instead of stopping at "it's wrong"?
y-m-68-06.s.s3.model.0: (x^n)′ = n·x^(n−1) is a rule for when the exponent n is a constant, but in x^x the exponent is also a variable, so it cannot be used as it is. At x = 1, ln 1 = 0, so B's formula also gives 1, and the value just happened to be the same as A's.
y-m-68-06.s.s3.model.1: A saw only the base as changing and treated the exponent x like a constant. The exponent also changes with x, but A did not reflect that change. The only point where the two formulas are equal is x = 1, so it looks right by coincidence only there.

y-m-68-07.title: Can we speak of the volume when we know only one side of the cross-section?
y-m-68-07.topic: Integration methods: the volume of a solid using the area of cross-sections (needed information and design)
y-m-68-07.goal: Learn that to fix the volume the area of the cross-section must be fixed as an expression in x, sort out whether the information about the cross-section shape is sufficient, and design in various ways a solid whose volume is exactly 16.
y-m-68-07.material: a is positive. There is a solid whose base is the plane figure enclosed by the curve y = √x, the x-axis, and the line x = a. The solid stands on this figure, and the cross-section made by cutting the solid with a plane perpendicular to the x-axis is a plane figure that has the segment on the base (length √x, 0 < x < a) as one side. The cross-section stands perpendicular to the base. All the units of length are the same. What figure the cross-section is has not been fixed yet.
y-m-68-07.thinking.2: Check a calculation that wrongly assumed how the area changes with x
y-m-68-07.prereq.0: The meaning that a definite integral is the value that adds up the amounts of thin slices
y-m-68-07.prereq.1: That √x can be seen as x^(1/2)
y-m-68-07.prereq.2: Assumption: during the integration methods unit of high school Calculus II (H3 is a difficulty classification of this set of tasks and does not mean assignment to a specific grade)
y-m-68-07.s.s1.prompt: What further information can you be given so that the volume can be written as an expression in a alone? Choose all the information that can do that.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.hint.0: For each option, try to write the area of the cross-section as an expression in x.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.hint.1: If you cannot write it, say what more value you would need to be able to.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.o.a: The cross-sections are all similar figures. (We do not know what shape.)
y-m-68-07.s.s1.r.a: If they are similar figures, the area has the form (one side)² times a fixed ratio, but if you do not know that ratio, you cannot write the volume in terms of a alone.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.r.b: If they are squares, the area is (√x)² = x, an expression in x alone.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.o.c: The perimeter of every cross-section is the same.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.r.c: Even if the perimeters are the same, if the shapes differ, the areas differ. You cannot fix the area.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.o.d: The cross-sections are all semicircles with that segment as the diameter.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.r.d: If the diameter is √x, the radius is √x/2, so the area is fixed as an expression in x alone.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.o.e: The cross-sections are all rectangles and the length of the other side is constant, but we do not know its value.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.r.e: If you do not know the length h of the other side, h remains in the volume formula, so it is not an expression in a alone.
y-m-68-07.s.s1.explain: The volume is the value that gathers the area of the cross-section A(x) from x = 0 to a, so A(x) has to be fixed as an expression in x alone. If squares, A(x) = x, so the volume is a²/2, and if semicircles, A(x) = πx/8, so the volume is πa²/16. Similar figures (ratio unknown), perimeter, and an unknown height do not fix the area.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.prompt: Now suppose the cross-sections are all rectangles, with the segment on the base (length √x) as one side and the length of the other side being a constant positive number h that does not depend on x. Make 3 pairs (a, h), with different a, for which the volume of the solid is exactly 16.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.hint.0: First write the area of the cross-section at x as the product of one side and the other side.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.hint.1: If you fix one a first and then match h, find what kind of number a makes a^(3/2) come out cleanly.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.fail.c1: a and h must be greater than 0.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The volume is not 16. Write the area of the cross-section as an expression in x and check again the value that gathers it from 0 to a.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.explain: The area of the cross-section is h√x, so the volume is (the value gathering h√x from x = 0 to a) = (2/3)·h·a^(3/2). (a, h) = (4, 3), (1, 24), (16, 0.375), (0.25, 192) and so on give a volume of 16. If you wrongly take the area to be h·x, then from h·a²/2 = 16 you get answers like (4, 2), but the actual volume of that is about 10.7, so it is wrong.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one of the (a, h) you made, write the area of the cross-section as an expression in x, and briefly explain the process of gathering it so that the volume becomes 16.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.because.hint.0: For the (a, h) you chose, write with specific numbers, at x = 1 and 4, how the area of the cross-section changes with x.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.because.hint.1: Recall how the phrase "stacking thin cross-sections" is written as an expression.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: the area of the cross-section at x is ...
y-m-68-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the area of the cross-section as an expression in x, like h·√x?
y-m-68-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you link the volume to "the value that gathers the area of the cross-section from 0 to a"?
y-m-68-07.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you substitute the (a, h) you chose directly and check that it gives 16?
y-m-68-07.s.s2.because.model.0: The area of the cross-section at x is h√x, one side √x times the other side h. Integrating this from x = 0 to a gives (2/3)·h·a^(3/2), and with a = 4 and h = 3, (2/3)·3·8 = 16.
y-m-68-07.s.s2.because.model.1: The area of the cross-section at x is h·√x, and stacking these thin cross-sections from 0 to a (integrating) gives a volume of (2/3)·h·a·√a. If a = 1, then (2/3)h = 16, so h = 24.

y-m-68-08.title: To a junior who says the derivative of sin 3x is cos 3x
y-m-68-08.topic: Various differentiation methods: explaining to a junior about the derivative of a function with an expression inside
y-m-68-08.goal: While respecting the misconception of a junior who has learned only Calculus I (seeing 3x as one block and using the formula as it is), write an explanation that includes a check the junior can do for themselves and the reason why that answer is wrong.
y-m-68-08.material: A junior who has learned only differentiation of polynomial functions and the derivative of sin x wrote the derivative of y = sin 3x like this: "(sin x)′ = cos x, so (sin 3x)′ = cos 3x." The junior thought that if you see 3x as one block it has the same shape as sin x. What the junior needs is not only to be told the right answer but a way to check it for themselves. (Read as: sine of 3x, cosine of 3x.)
y-m-68-08.thinking.0: Analyze the cause of a misconception
y-m-68-08.thinking.1: Sort out ways of checking that can be verified
y-m-68-08.thinking.2: Change an explanation to take into account what the audience (the junior) does not know
y-m-68-08.prereq.0: That the derivative of sin x is cos x
y-m-68-08.prereq.1: The meaning that the value of a derivative is the slope of the tangent line drawn to the graph
y-m-68-08.prereq.2: Assumption: after learning the differentiation unit of high school Calculus II (H3 is a difficulty classification of this set of tasks and does not mean assignment to a specific grade)
y-m-68-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the fitting ways to help the junior confirm for themselves that the answer is wrong.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write what the slope at x = 0 would have to be if the junior's answer cos 3x were right.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.hint.1: For each option, work out whether it is a check the junior can do themselves and whether that check can show that the junior's answer is wrong.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.o.a: Have them reread (sin x)′ = cos x in the textbook and confirm that 3x can be used just like x.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.r.a: Rereading the formula does not confirm whether 3x plays the same role as x. There is no way to test the answer.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.o.b: Show that sin 3x = 3 sin x and have them pull the 3 out front.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.r.b: sin 3x = 3 sin x does not hold. For example, if x = π/6, then sin(π/2) = 1 and 3 sin(π/6) = 1.5.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.o.c: Have them calculate (sin 3h − sin 0)/h for a small h near x = 0 and compare it with cos 0 = 1.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.r.c: This had them test the answer with a value they can calculate themselves.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.o.d: Explain that y = sin 3x is also a sine-curve shape, so its slope is also the same as y = sin x.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.r.d: Even if the shape is a sine curve, if it is squeezed horizontally it becomes steeper. Saying it is the same shape does not guarantee the same slope.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.o.e: Have them recall that the graph of y = sin 3x is the graph of y = sin x squeezed horizontally to one third, and think about how the slope changes when it is squeezed.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.r.e: This had them find a reason for the slope to change from the change in the shape of the graph.
y-m-68-08.s.s1.explain: If h = 0.01, sin(0.03)/0.01 ≈ 2.9996, so the slope at x = 0 is about 3, not cos 0 = 1. If you squeeze the graph horizontally to one third, the same change in height happens 3 times as fast, so the slope also becomes 3 times as large. The junior can try these two methods for themselves. Rereading the formula or an explanation that only the shape is the same cannot sift out the wrong answer.
y-m-68-08.s.s2.prompt: Write a message to send to the junior. (3 to 5 sentences) Include the correct derivative, why it is not cos 3x, and one check the junior can do for themselves. Do not use terms the junior has not learned yet.
y-m-68-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write in separate lines the part of the junior's idea that is right and the part that does not fit.
y-m-68-08.s.s2.hint.1: Make a table with a few small numbers showing how much the value of sin 3x changes when x changes a little near x = 0.

y-m-68-08.s.s2.model.0: It is right that the derivative of sin x is cos x. But in sin 3x, when x goes up by 1, the 3x inside goes up by 3, so it changes 3 times as fast, and the derivative is 3cos 3x. To check, put in a small value 0.01 near x = 0 and calculate sin(0.03)/0.01. You get about 3, which is different from the 1 you get by putting 0 into cos 3x.
y-m-68-08.s.s2.model.1: It is not cos 3x. The graph of y = sin 3x is y = sin x squeezed horizontally to one third, so the slope becomes 3 times as steep. So the derivative is 3cos 3x. To check, find the slope of the graph at x = 0 from two nearby points and see whether you get 1 or 3.
